tagline.text: A Catholic heritage museum in the rebuilt San Ignacio Church and Jesuit Mission House

location.label: Location
location.text: Corner of Arzobispo and Anda Streets, Intramuros, Manila

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱150–600 (admission, transport and snacks, half-day basis)

children.text: A museum of church art rebuilt on the site of San Ignacio Church in Intramuros. Inside the reconstructed Jesuit Mission House, six galleries show saint images, colonial religious paintings and silver liturgical objects from the Intramuros Administration's collection.

Museo de Intramuros is an ecclesiastical museum at the corner of Arzobispo and Anda Streets in Intramuros, Manila's walled city. The building is a reconstruction of the San Ignacio Church built by the Jesuits and of the Jesuit Mission House (Casa Misión). It is run by the Intramuros Administration and displays the Catholic-themed collection the administration has gathered over many years.

The original San Ignacio Church was designed in the Neoclassical style by architect Félix Roxas Sr., and its interior was reportedly carved in dark hardwood by Isabelo Tampinco. It was destroyed in the 1945 Battle of Manila and is said to have burned for four days, partly because so much kamagong hardwood was used. The site was later used as offices, a warehouse and a basketball court, until excavation and restoration planning began after the Intramuros Administration was founded in 1979. Excavations carried out with the National Museum turned up about 500 artifacts.

Construction of the museum began in 2009. The Mission House was blessed in January 2018 and first opened in February of that year for the Manila Biennale exhibition. The permanent exhibits were reported to have opened officially in early May 2019. Admission was announced as free for the first six months, but it is now paid, so check the costs table below and the latest announcements.
The exhibits are built around the question of
how Spanish evangelization was received by Filipinos

. By looking at saint images, religious paintings and silver liturgical objects, you can slowly read how colonial-era Catholic faith took shape in this land. It is a good place to rest for an hour or two in the middle of a day walking around Intramuros. The museum is not large, so about an hour is enough if you only skim it, but reading the labels and studying the iconography of each statue can take close to two hours. If you are interested in Catholic faith or Spanish colonial art, it is a stop you should not miss in Intramuros, and even visitors new to religious art can follow the explanations and easily grasp one side of Philippine history.

The heart of the museum is the rebuilt Jesuit Mission House. It gives a sense of the scale of a colonial-era clergy residence, so the building is as much a sight as the exhibits. The Mission House was completed in 2018 and opened to the public in 2019.

The first theme is the Immaculate Conception. According to the Intramuros Administration's official description, the "Imagenes/Indigena" exhibit presents evangelization from the point of view of the Filipino people (indios). Centered on images of the Virgin, it shows how the faith was interpreted locally.

The religious orders gallery gathers images of saints associated with each order and adds notes on their iconography. Once you know what the objects a saint holds and the clothes they wear mean, the statues you see in churches look different too.

The courtyard gallery covers the Spanish crown's mission patronage (Patronato Real) and how churches were built in the towns of the reducción era. It gives useful background if you like to visit old churches around the Philippines.
"Larawan" is the gallery on religious colonial paintings. It explains what role religious paintings played in evangelization and how Spanish styles changed in the hands of local painters.

The "Sacramento" gallery explains the importance of the main altar and shows silver sacred objects made by Chinese and Filipino silversmiths. You can get close to the craftsmanship in small items such as chalices and censers.
The last gallery pulls the earlier themes together. It looks once more at how Filipinos accepted the faith the Spanish brought and reshaped it.

About 500 artifacts came out of the San Ignacio site, and among them the "Intramuros Pot Shard" is known as an ancient inscribed artifact recovered through systematic excavation. Whether it is on display may vary over time, so please ask on site.

items.title: Half-day museum visit
items.subtitle: Seeing the church and museum in Intramuros

children.text: Arrive when the museum opens. Hours may change, so check the Intramuros Administration's announcements before you come.
Buy your ticket at the counter and start with the ground-floor galleries of the Mission House. See the Immaculate Conception exhibit and the saints of the religious orders first.
Visit the courtyard gallery on church building and royal patronage. Then move on to the galleries of paintings and silver liturgical objects.
After the last gallery, ask the staff about the passage to the neighboring building and the nearby Centro de Turismo.
Have lunch at a restaurant nearby in Intramuros. In the afternoon, continue to San Agustin Church, Manila Cathedral and Casa Manila.
If you are walking all of Intramuros in one day, it works best to place this museum in the midday heat as an indoor break.

items.title: One day in Intramuros
items.subtitle: A walk through churches, the museum and the fort

children.text: Start at Fort Santiago at the northern end of the walls and walk in the cool early air.
See San Agustin Church and its museum, then move to the plaza in front of Manila Cathedral.
Arrive at Museo de Intramuros and take your time with the sacred art. This is the indoor rest stop during the hottest hours.
Eat lunch at a restaurant inside the walls and rest for a while.
Finish with Casa Manila or a walk along the walls, then watch the sea view toward Roxas Boulevard around sunset before heading back to your hotel.
The official opening hours have differed over time, so when planning a full day, keep the museum as the flexible part of your schedule.

From within Manila, the easiest way to reach the Intramuros gate (such as the Puerta Real or Aduana-side entrances) is by taxi or Grab. The museum's address is the corner of Arzobispo and Anda Streets.
From Makati or BGC, it can take about
40 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes
depending on traffic. It is best to avoid rush hours.
You can also get off at an LRT-1 station and walk into the walled city, but given the heat and the walking distance, first check the nearest station and the walking distance on a map app.
From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) you can go by Grab or taxi. It takes about
30 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes
depending on traffic.
Rather than coming straight from the airport, it is more comfortable to drop your bags at your hotel first. We have not confirmed whether the museum can store large bags, so ask on site.
Intramuros is small enough to explore on foot, and there are bicycle rentals and kalesa (horse-drawn carriages). Check the price before you use them and bargain.
The San Ignacio site is close to Manila Cathedral and San Agustin Church, so it is common to walk them together.
The museum is indoors and can be visited on rainy days, so it depends less on the season, but if you are walking all of Intramuros, the dry season is far more comfortable.

During the day, opening time and late afternoon are cooler. Weekends can be crowded with group tours and school trips, and the official guidance once said Tuesday to Friday visits were by appointment only, so check the date first.

There are not many hotels inside Intramuros, so many visitors come from Malate or Ermita in Manila, or from Makati. If you want to stay inside the walls, check the location and noise level before booking.
You can have lunch at a Filipino restaurant or café inside the walls. We have not confirmed whether food is sold inside the museum, so use the nearby restaurants.

After the museum, it is nice to stroll the streets inside the walls and try Filipino snacks. Prices and opening hours differ from shop to shop, so check before you go in. The walled city gets quiet in the evening, so it is safer to walk out to the main road outside the walls and call a taxi or Grab before dark.
Check the days and hours on the Intramuros Administration's official page before you visit. At one time, Tuesday to Friday was announced as by appointment only.
The admission fee differs between the official page and other guides. Bring enough cash, since cards or e-wallets may not work.
You need ID to get a discount. Carry your actual student or senior ID rather than a copy.
Group visits are advised to be booked at least 2 days ahead.
Inside the walls, starting early in the morning keeps you from the heat. Placing the museum at midday makes a good rest.
Exhibit explanations may be mainly in English and Filipino. Learning a little about saints' names and iconography beforehand makes it easier to follow.
Comparing it with the museum at San Agustin Church gives you a broader understanding of faith-based art in the Spanish colonial period.
Fee and opening-hour information differs by source. Be sure to check the Intramuros Administration's announcements before you go.
The church and museum have the character of a religious site, so avoid revealing clothing and visit quietly.
Do not touch the exhibits or glass display cases. Follow the on-site instructions on photography rules.
Intramuros is very hot by day with little shade. Bring water, a hat and sunscreen.
Watch out for pickpockets and touts, and agree on the fare before riding a kalesa or bicycle.
Stone floors can be slippery on rainy days.
About
5–10 minutes
on foot, this is Manila's main cathedral. Seeing it together with the museum links up the story of religious architecture.
About
10 minutes
on foot, this is a UNESCO World Heritage church. You can see the setting behind the museum's exhibits with your own eyes.
A fort at the northern end of the walls, within walking distance of the museum. It is a place where traces of José Rizal remain.
The museum is one part of the walled city of Intramuros. For a full route around the walls, see the Intramuros entry.
